title: Milinda's chariot, alone
hookLine: read the chariot dialogue whole (Milinda, Book 2)
tomorrow: what did the hare in the moon give away?

lines: WHO ARE YOU, IN ONE LINE?
cards: Every profile wants a bio. Who are you, in one line: artist, student, runner, overthinker. Pick one, and by Thursday it feels like a lie.
In the Questions of King Milinda, a king meets a monk named Nagasena and asks his name. I'm called Nagasena, the monk says, but that's only a name. No person is found here.
The king pounces. Then who is talking to me? Who keeps the precepts?

teach.b: Is your hair Nagasena, the king asks? Your nails, your skin, your feelings? No, each time.
Then Nagasena is just a sound, and you've lied. Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks: how did you come here, your majesty?
Then show me the chariot. Is it the pole? The axle?
The wheels, the frame, the reins? None of them. All the parts in a heap?
No. Something apart from the parts? No.
Then there's no chariot, and you've lied.
The king, caught, gives the answer himself: chariot is the name we use when those parts come together. Exactly, says Nagasena. So is Nagasena.

And he quotes a nun, Sister Vajira: as the word chariot is used for an assembly of parts, so we speak of a being when the parts of a person are there. This is the Buddhist teaching of anatta, not-self.
It doesn't say you're nothing; the king did arrive in something.
It says there's no fixed core hiding under the parts: body, feeling, perception, habits of mind, awareness, all changing together, with a name that's still useful. And that turns out to be freeing.
A chariot of parts can be repaired.

how: Buddhist teachers use Nagasena's chariot to explain anatta, not-self, and meditators practice looking at body, feeling, perception, mental habits and awareness as changing parts rather than a fixed self.

o: the war chariot a Greek king gave to the Buddha
a parable about racing toward awakening quickly
a monk's proof that a self is a name for parts

games.q: inside the dialogue — tap the pairs.
p: a king who asks a monk his name
the nun whose chariot line he quotes

s: Nagasena teaches that people don't exist at all
the chariot is real enough to ride in; chariot is the name used for the parts together, and so is a person's name.
the chariot line Nagasena quotes comes from a nun
Sister Vajira: as chariot names an assembly of parts, so being names the parts of a person.
not-self means you shouldn't care what happens to you
the teaching drops a fixed core, not care: a chariot of parts can still be looked after and repaired.

games.q: your friend says, "i've always been a bad test-taker. it's just who i am." how would Nagasena's chariot answer?
o: "bad test-taker" names parts, like nerves and habits, and parts can change
deep down there's a true self that's great at tests; go find it
since there's no self, it doesn't really matter how she does
games.why: a name like chariot or bad test-taker is used for parts working together. there's no fixed core under them, and that's exactly why they can change.

practice: Pick up one object near you, a cup, a pen, your phone, and name its parts slowly, one per breath, until you can't find the cup among them. Set it down, still a cup.
Then, more gently, do the same with the word I: a body, a feeling, a thought passing, the knowing of it, and let the name rest lightly on all of them.

wordCard.voice: Milinda's chariot: Nagasena's answer to a king. Chariot is a name for parts working together, and so is the name of a person.

orig.note: Pali: not-self; no fixed core under the parts of a person.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a chariot of parts, and parts can always be repaired. Chariot parked.
